item.title: The utilitarian temptation in gene editing | Science
item.description: The recent gene-editing trial led by Zilong Qiu and colleagues in Shanghai (“A fatal reaction,” B. Borrell, News Feature, 23 July, 10.1126/science.aek8000) was not only a case of failed oversight; it also illustrates a recurring moral danger in biomedical research. Such trials can be driven by two mutually reinforcing motivations: the pursuit of professional recognition and a crude utilitarian rationale that risky experiments are justified because, if successful, they may benefit large numbers of present and future patients. This second motivation, which is especially powerful in biomedicine, can cloak self-interest in moral language and encourage researchers to discount evidence of danger to the individuals enrolled as subjects. Gene-editing interventions, in particular, may appear morally elevated because their promised benefits aim to enhance general welfare for all, including future generations, regardless of nationality or group identity. For this reason, the appeal to future benefit requires strict ethical limits.

item.title: Streamlining oversight in gene-editing trials | Science
item.description: In the News Feature “A fatal reaction” (23 July, 10.1126/science. aek8000), B. Borrell reports that a 6-year-old girl died after the world’s first-in-human brain base-editing trial in China. This case highlights a governance paradox: A regulatory system with detailed ethical rules failed to prevent a fatal outcome. Institutional fragmentation may be at fault. As countries expand access to highly individualized gene-editing therapies, they must also strengthen continuous, cross-institutional oversight.

item.title: Recording results from single-patient trials | Science
item.description: In the News Feature “A fatal reaction” (23 July, 10.1126/science.aek8000), B. Borrell reports that a 6-year-old child died 7 days after receiving an individualized base-editing treatment. Although the girl was the only participant that the trial intended to enroll, the registry continued to describe the study as “recruiting” more than a year later (1). During the same period, the related preclinical study cited nonhuman-primate delivery as evidence of translational feasibility (2) but did not mention the human trial. To ensure that the results of single-patient research are preserved, relevant protocols and major human outcomes should be recorded and kept current in a public registry.
